n: The book of Alma opens in the first year of the reign of the judges (about 91 BC). Mosiah has died — “gone the way of all the earth” — but his laws remain, accepted by the people and binding on them.

f.w: gone the way of all the earth

n: In Alma’s first year as chief judge, a large, notably strong man is brought before him for trial.

f.g: The office of chief judge; Alma is both chief judge and high priest.

n: This man had been preaching against the church, teaching that religious leaders should seek popularity and be paid by the people rather than work for their own living.

f.g: The opposite of the Nephite church’s practice of unpaid, self-supporting leaders.

n: His doctrine was attractive: everyone will be saved no matter what, so no one needs to fear, repent, or change. It offered comfort without accountability.

f.w: all mankind should be saved at the last day
f.g: A form of universalism; compare the false teachings warned against in 2 Nephi 28:7-8.

n: His message became popular enough that many believers began paying him.
Success fed his pride. He began dressing in expensive clothes and founded a church built around his own teachings.

f.g: In the Book of Mormon, expensive clothing often signals pride.

n: On his way to preach he met a teacher of the church and argued hard, hoping to win church members away. The teacher stood firm, answering with God’s word.

f.w: admonishing him with the words of God

n: The teacher was Gideon — the same man who years earlier had helped free Limhi’s people from bondage.
Angry at being opposed, the man drew his sword and attacked Gideon. Gideon, now very old, could not defend himself and was killed.
Church members seized the killer and brought him to Alma for judgment.

f.w: to be judged according to the crimes
f.g: He is tried for murder under civil law, not for his beliefs.

n: He defended himself boldly before Alma.

f.g: Pleaded his case; argued in his own defense.

n: Alma names the crime: priestcraft, now introduced among the Nephites for the first time — and worse, enforced by the sword. If allowed to spread, it would destroy the nation.

f.g: Preaching for one’s own gain and praise rather than for the welfare of others.

n: Alma explains that the man had killed a righteous, deeply respected man. To let him go would make the whole people guilty of Gideon’s blood.

f.w: his blood would come upon us

n: Alma sentences him to death under Mosiah’s law, which the people had accepted. The sentence is for murder, not for teaching false doctrine.

f.w: the law which has been given us by Mosiah

n: His name was Nehor. Before his execution on the hill Manti, he admitted that his teachings had been contrary to God’s word, and he died a shameful death.

f.g: His “order” of teaching will trouble the Nephites for generations.

n: Nehor’s death did not stop priestcraft. Many who loved worldly things went on preaching false doctrines for money and honor.

f.w: for the sake of riches and honor

n: These preachers could not openly lie, for lying was punished, so they claimed to preach their sincere beliefs. Belief itself could not be punished under the law.

f.w: the law could have no power on any man for his belief

n: Likewise they did not dare steal, rob, or murder — such crimes were punished, and murder by death.
Those outside the church began persecuting those who had taken Christ’s name.

f.w: taken upon them the name of Christ

n: They mocked and harassed believers for their humility and because members freely shared God’s word without charging money.
The church had a strict rule: members must not persecute non-members, nor one another.
Yet some members grew proud and fought back with their fists — failing the test of persecution in a different way.
This happened in Alma’s second year as judge and caused the church great trouble.
Many hardened their hearts and were removed from church records, and others simply left.
This was hard on the faithful, but they stayed steadfast and immovable, patiently enduring persecution.
A picture of the ideal church: priests and people paused their work to hear God’s word, then all went back to work. Preacher and hearer, teacher and learner, were equals.

f.w: the preacher was no better than the hearer
f.g: The direct opposite of Nehor’s idea that priests should be elevated and supported.

n: They shared what they had with the poor, needy, sick, and afflicted. They dressed simply but neatly, avoiding showy clothing.
By living this way, the church enjoyed continued peace despite persecution.
Because of their steadiness, they became very prosperous, with abundant livestock, grain, precious metals, and fine cloth.
Their prosperity did not make them selfish. They helped anyone in need — old or young, slave or free, member or not — without favoritism. This is how wealth should be used.
They became far wealthier than those outside the church.
Outsiders, by contrast, gave themselves to sorcery, idolatry, idleness, gossip, envy, pride, and many crimes. The law was enforced against lawbreakers as much as possible.
Consistent enforcement of the law made the wicked quieter, and the Nephites had peace until the fifth year of the judges.
